title: The House of Children: from the Tenements of San Lorenzo to the Grave at Noordwijk
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Chiaravalle to Rome: the Engineer's Daughter

stops.name: Chiaravalle, the birth on Piazza Mazzini
stops.date_confidence: attested; town coordinates corrected to 43.600, 13.333 per it.wikipedia, and the pin set on the birth house at Piazza Mazzini 10, which the research pool had misplaced by about eight kilometres
stops.campa: At number 10 of Piazza Mazzini, in a Marche town of beet fields and hemp behind Ancona, Alessandro Montessori of the state financial administration and Renilde Stoppani have their only child, and name her Maria Tecla Artemisia. The Kingdom of Italy is nine years old and the province was papal within living memory. Renilde Stoppani's family name will follow her daughter into every biography written since. The house carries a bronze plaque now, and a museum. Nothing in the register of births distinguishes it from its neighbours on the square.
suggested_refs: The birth house at Piazza Mazzini 10, Chiaravalle, now the museum of the Fondazione Chiaravalle-Montessori

stops.name: Florence, the ministry moves the family north
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Alessandro's work carries the household to Florence, capital of Italy until three years ago and still full of the ministries that made it one. Maria is three. The record of these years is thin: no school, no anecdote, nothing but a family following a civil servant's postings from one rented address to the next. She will see the city again once, seventy-seven years later. Two years after this the same work carries them to Rome, and Rome will hold her for the whole of her working life. Of Florence itself no source consulted here has found a mark, left on her or by her.
suggested_refs: Alessandro Montessori's service record with the state financial administration

stops.name: Rome, the family settles and the child enters school
stops.date_confidence: attested; the move is dated 1875 and the school entry 1876, the two compressed into one stop
stops.campa: The Montessoris take a house in Rome, and in 1876 the six-year-old enters a public elementary school. What survives of that schooling is a set of certificates: one for conduct, one for needlework. The prodigy stories came later, supplied by a movement that wanted a childhood to match the woman. The girl in the documents is a competent ordinary pupil in an ordinary Roman classroom, sitting at a fixed bench bolted to the floor of a room she is not free to cross.
suggested_refs: Montessori's Roman elementary school certificates for conduct and needlework

stops.name: Rome, the technical schools and the turn away from engineering
stops.date_confidence: attested to the years 1883 to 1890; en.wikipedia describes two successive institutions, while it.wikipedia treats the Regia Scuola Tecnica and the Istituto Tecnico Leonardo da Vinci as one school renamed, a contradiction left standing
stops.campa: At thirteen she enters the Regia Scuola Tecnica Michelangelo Buonarroti, a school built for boys, and studies Italian, history, geography, mathematics, accounting and science. From 1886 she continues at the Regio Istituto Tecnico Leonardo da Vinci, adding drawing, physics, chemistry, botany and zoology, and completes the physics and mathematics course in 1890. She has been aiming at engineering. In her last year she changes her mind and settles on medicine, a faculty which in Italy has admitted almost no women at all.
suggested_refs: The Regio Istituto Tecnico Leonardo da Vinci, Rome, its physics and mathematics course of 1886 to 1890

segments.name: The Degree No Woman Was Meant to Take

stops.name: Rome, the Sapienza and the long way round to medicine
stops.date_confidence: attested to the years 1890 and 1892; the papal-intervention story is tradition, unsupported by any document in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Medicine is not open to her directly, so she goes round it. She enrols at the University of Rome in natural sciences, physics, chemistry, botany, zoology, and in 1892 takes the diploma di licenza that qualifies a candidate for the medical faculty. Two years of the long way about. Movement lore holds that Pope Leo XIII intervened in person to open the door for her, and no document supports it; the paperwork shows a young woman climbing an ordinary academic staircase one required certificate at a time, in the order the statutes prescribe.
suggested_refs: The Palazzo della Sapienza, seat of the University of Rome in the 1890s

stops.name: Rome, the dissecting room after hours
stops.date_confidence: 1893 attested as the start of formal medical study; the solitary dissections and the smoking are movement tradition recorded by later biographers, with no contemporaneous documentation found
stops.campa: She begins formal medical study. The story her students told afterwards is that propriety forbade her to stand over a naked cadaver in the presence of men, so she was sent to dissect alone in the evenings, and that she took up smoking to cover the formaldehyde. It rests on recollection rather than on any contemporaneous record. What the record does hold is that she finishes the course in a faculty where the presence of a woman is a standing question, raised by colleagues and by their families, and that she does not leave it.
suggested_refs: The anatomical theatre of the University of Rome medical faculty, 1890s

stops.name: Rome, the degree in medicine
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1896; day not recorded, defaulted to the first
stops.campa: In July she takes her degree and becomes one of the first women in Italy to qualify as a physician. Not the first: Ernestina Paper had qualified at Florence nineteen years earlier, a fact the movement's own literature has been careless with for a century. She goes into private practice and into the university psychiatric clinic, and begins visiting the asylums of Rome, where among the adults she finds children classified as deficient, shut in bare rooms, with nothing whatever to do with their hands.
suggested_refs: The asylums of Rome visited from the university psychiatric clinic, 1896 onward

stops.name: Berlin, the congress and the wage
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1896; day not recorded, defaulted to the first
stops.campa: Two months out of the medical faculty she is sent to Berlin to represent Italy at the International Congress for Women's Rights, and speaks on the labour of women and the pay of women. She moves that the wages of workers be brought to one level, male or female, and puts the principle in a phrase short enough for the delegates to carry home. The German press covers the Italian woman doctor rather more closely than it covers her motion. She is twenty-six.
stops.quote: the same wage for the same work
stops.quote_source: Montessori at the International Congress for Women's Rights, Berlin, September 1896, per the AMI Montessori Archives
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the 1896 International Congress for Women's Rights, Berlin
sources: AMI Montessori Archives, '1896 International Congress for Women's Rights'

stops.name: Turin, the two congresses and one argument
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1897 for the National Medical Congress and 1898 for the First Pedagogical Conference; months not recorded, the two compressed into one stop at the shared city
stops.campa: Twice within two years she stands before the Italian congresses at Turin and argues the same thing from two directions. To the National Medical Congress she says that juvenile crime grows out of social neglect and not out of an inborn criminal nature. To the First Pedagogical Conference she says that the children the state calls deficient need institutions of their own and teachers trained for them. Both arguments are moral. Both are dressed, as the decade requires, in the vocabulary of medicine.
suggested_refs: Acts of the Italian National Medical Congress, Turin 1897, and of the First Pedagogical Conference, Turin 1898

stops.name: Rome, the birth of Mario
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the last day of March she gives birth to a son by her colleague Giuseppe Montesano. The child is registered as Mario Pipilli, parents unknown, and boarded with a family in the country outside the city. She does not marry, does not acknowledge him publicly for years, and does not stop working; the alternative is the end of the career she has just spent eight years building. He will come to her as a young man, take her name, run her organisation, share an internment with her in India, and be in the house when she dies.
suggested_refs: The Roman civil birth register entry for Mario Pipilli, 31 March 1898

segments.name: Itard, Seguin, and the Orthophrenic School

stops.name: Paris, the two physicians of the idiot and the wild boy
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1899; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: She goes to Paris to read Jean Itard and Edouard Seguin, the physicians who tried to educate the wild boy of Aveyron and the children the asylums had written off. Their method is an apparatus: graded objects for the hand, sorted by size and weight and roughness, teaching the senses one distinction at a time. Seguin took the equipment for a treatment of deficiency. Montessori carries it away convinced it is a description of how any child at all comes to know anything, which is not what either man wrote.
suggested_refs: Edouard Seguin, Traitement moral, hygiene et education des idiots (1846); Jean Itard's reports on Victor of Aveyron

stops.name: London, the Council of Women and the Sicilian mines
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1899; month and day not recorded, defaulted here to June for ordering within the year
stops.campa: At the International Council of Women in London she speaks about women workers and about the children in the sulphur mines of Sicily, and is presented with the other delegates to Queen Victoria, who is eighty. The London papers take an interest in the woman doctor from Rome. Eight years before the first Casa dei Bambini, she is already a public figure in two languages, an authority on labour, on delinquency and on the education of the disabled. She has published nothing at all about ordinary children.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the International Council of Women, London 1899

stops.name: Rome, the Orthophrenic School
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1900; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: She is made co-director, with Montesano, of a new state school for training teachers of children with disabilities, and takes a class of the children herself. For two years she works with them from eight in the morning to seven at night, making and remaking the Seguin materials, watching what a hand does when it is given something exact to do. Some of her pupils sit the state examinations set for ordinary children and pass. Rome reads this as a triumph over deficiency. She reads it as a verdict on the schools.
stops.quote: Child psychology can be established only through the method of external observation.
stops.quote_source: Maria Montessori, The Montessori Method (1912), ch. IV
suggested_refs: The Scuola Magistrale Ortofrenica, Rome, founded 1900

stops.name: Rome, the free lectureship and the measuring of children
stops.date_confidence: 1904 attested for the libera docente; the date she gave up medicine is contested, Wikipedia dating the departure from the Orthophrenic School and private practice to 1901 and the university resignation to 1919, while the AMI timeline puts the abandonment of medicine at 1911
stops.campa: She leaves the Orthophrenic School and her private practice and returns to the university as a student again: philosophy, psychology, anthropology. In 1904 she qualifies as libera docente in anthropology and lectures four years in pedagogical anthropology, measuring the skulls, the chests and the heights of Roman schoolchildren and filling notebooks with the anthropometry her generation took for the science of education. The Casa dei Bambini comes out of this room. It does not come out of any change of heart about it.
suggested_refs: Montessori's course in pedagogical anthropology, University of Rome, 1904 to 1908
sources: AMI Montessori Archives, 'Timeline: Maria Montessori's Life'

segments.name: San Lorenzo: the House of Children

stops.name: San Lorenzo, Talamo's tenements
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1906; month and day not recorded. Talamo's role is standard in the literature and in the Stanford Encyclopedia entry, but his name does not appear in the current en.wikipedia text cited by the research pool
stops.campa: A Roman building company has bought and renovated the tenement blocks of San Lorenzo, a quarter of labourers thrown up fast and badly outside the old walls. Its manager, Edoardo Talamo, has a practical problem: the small children of his tenants, too young for school, spend the working day on the stairs and the walls while their parents are out. He asks the woman who lectures on pedagogical anthropology to put them somewhere indoors. She is thirty-six. The offer is caretaking, and she takes it.
suggested_refs: The Istituto Romano dei Beni Stabili tenement blocks of San Lorenzo, renovated 1906

stops.name: San Lorenzo, the first Casa dei Bambini
stops.date_confidence: attested to 6 January 1907; the street number is disputed, the AMI timeline giving Via dei Marsi 53 and secondary literature 58, while en.wikipedia gives no number at all. Ages follow en.wikipedia, two or three to six or seven
stops.campa: On the Feast of the Epiphany a room on Via dei Marsi opens with fifty or sixty children of two or three to six or seven, the porter's daughter to mind them, and a set of materials carried over from the asylum work. She has the tables and chairs cut down to the size of the people using them and the cupboards hung where a child can reach. Then she watches, and writes down what happens when nobody makes them do anything. They choose. They repeat the same thing forty times. They go quiet.
stops.quote: The "Children's House" is the environment which is offered to the child that he may be given the opportunity of developing his activities.
stops.quote_source: Maria Montessori, Dr. Montessori's Own Handbook (1914), opening of 'A Children's House'
suggested_refs: The first Casa dei Bambini, Via dei Marsi, San Lorenzo, opened 6 January 1907
sources: AMI Montessori Archives, 'Timeline: Maria Montessori's Life'

stops.name: San Lorenzo, the second house and the visitors
stops.date_confidence: attested to 7 April 1907
stops.campa: A second Casa opens in the same quarter in April. Word of the first has travelled out of San Lorenzo and up into the drawing rooms; ambassadors, journalists and eventually queens come to stand at the back of a room of slum children and watch them polish brass and trace sandpaper letters without speaking. The classroom is now two things at once, a laboratory and a show, and the woman who has spent ten years insisting that the child must be observed does not close the door on the observers.
stops.quote: Collective discipline is obtained as if by magic force.
stops.quote_source: Maria Montessori, The Montessori Method (1912), on the silence exercise
suggested_refs: The second Casa dei Bambini, San Lorenzo, opened 7 April 1907

stops.name: Citta di Castello, the first course and the book
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1909; month and day not recorded. The explicit break with Froebel is a reconstruction from the standard history of early-childhood education, corroborated in the literature but not verified here against the 1909 Italian text
stops.campa: In a hill town in Umbria she gives her first training course for teachers, and the lectures go into type the same year with S. Lapi as Il Metodo della Pedagogia Scientifica applicato all'educazione infantile nelle Case dei Bambini. The book is long, argumentative and full of measurement, and it takes its distance from Friedrich Froebel by name: no gifts handed down by an adult, no symbolic play, no make-believe standing in for real work with real objects. Within three years it is a bestseller in English.
stops.quote: It is a conquest of liberty which the school needs, not the mechanism of a bench.
stops.quote_source: Maria Montessori, The Montessori Method (1912), on the stationary school desk
suggested_refs: Il Metodo della Pedagogia Scientifica, S. Lapi, Citta di Castello, 1909; froebel.journey.json for the kindergarten gifts the book argues against

stops.name: Milan, the anthropology in print
stops.date_confidence: 1910 attested for the publication of Antropologia pedagogica through the Wikipedia bibliography; the characterisation of its anthropometric and racial-hierarchy content is a reconstruction from the period's positivist anthropology, not verified here page by page
stops.campa: Her university lectures are published as Antropologia pedagogica, and they contain what her generation of positivist anthropology contained: skull measurement, body indices, a hierarchy of races taken for settled science. It is the same instrument she turned on the children of San Lorenzo, pointed where the discipline pointed it. Her admirers have generally preferred the other book. The following year she holds a third training course here in Milan, as the method runs out through Italy and beyond it.
suggested_refs: Maria Montessori, Antropologia pedagogica (1910)

stops.name: New York, the lecture tour
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1913; day not recorded. Which American school was first is disputed: en.wikipedia's Montessori article gives Tarrytown, October 1911, while its Montessori education article gives the Scarborough School, founded 1913 by Narcissa Cox Vanderlip and Frank A. Vanderlip. Neither Tarrytown nor the Bell household is staged here as a stop, since Montessori was at neither
stops.campa: The method reaches America before she does. A school opens at Tarrytown in the autumn of 1911, Alexander Graham Bell and Mabel Hubbard Bell open a class of their own and take up the presidency of an American Montessori association, and Anne George's translation sells like a novel. In December Montessori lands in New York for a lecture tour, speaking in Italian to audiences who cannot follow a word of it, and fills halls in Washington, Philadelphia, Boston, Pittsburgh and Chicago.
stops.quote: Our little ones have the impression of continually "making discoveries" in the world about them; and in this they find the greatest joy.
stops.quote_source: Maria Montessori, Dr. Montessori's Own Handbook (1914), 'Language'
suggested_refs: Anne E. George's translation, The Montessori Method (New York, 1912); alexander_graham_bell.journey.json for the Bells' Montessori patronage

stops.name: San Francisco, the classroom with glass walls
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1915; the exposition ran from February to December and no month is given for her visit, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: At the Panama-Pacific International Exposition a classroom is built with walls of glass. Helen Parkhurst, her trainee, runs the room, and Montessori gives a California training course the same year and does not object to the arrangement: the demonstration is the argument, and the argument requires witnesses. The American vogue is at its height on this fairground and will be over within three years. Inside the glass the children work; outside it the fairgoing public watches from tiered seats.
stops.quote: The spontaneous discipline, and the obedience which is seen in the whole class, constitute the most striking result of our method.
stops.quote_source: Maria Montessori, Dr. Montessori's Own Handbook (1914)
suggested_refs: The glass-walled Montessori classroom at the Panama-Pacific International Exposition, San Francisco, 1915

segments.name: Barcelona, the Duce, and the Closing of Europe

stops.name: Barcelona, the base of twenty years
stops.date_confidence: 1916 attested. The research pool credited the Mancomunitat de Catalunya, which appears in neither cited source and was suppressed in 1925, so it cannot underwrite the whole span; the AMI timeline attributes the invitation to the city government
stops.campa: She crosses back to a Europe at war and settles in Barcelona at the invitation of the city's authorities, who give her a school and a laboratory. Here the method grows upward out of the nursery: elementary material for children to twelve, arithmetic, grammar, geometry, the first sketches of what she will later call cosmic education. Barcelona is her home for twenty years, and they are not quiet years. A military directory closes her model school in 1924; the Republic pays for a fresh course in 1933.
stops.quote: To-day, he who speaks of liberty in the schools ought at the same time to exhibit objects--approximating to a scientific apparatus--which will make such liberty possible.
stops.quote_source: Maria Montessori, Spontaneous Activity in Education (The Advanced Montessori Method, vol. I), ch. III
suggested_refs: The Escola Montessori and pedagogical laboratory at Barcelona, 1916 to 1936
sources: AMI Montessori Archives, 'Timeline: Maria Montessori's Life'

stops.name: Amsterdam, the Dutch society
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1917; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: She lectures in Amsterdam and a Netherlands Montessori Society is founded the same year, among the first national bodies to organise around her name. She has no way of knowing that this small northern country will be the last one, that it will hold her archive, her headquarters and her grave. For now it is one foothold among many in a decade of them: societies, courses, translations, national associations multiplying faster than one woman in her forties can supervise. She goes back to Barcelona.
suggested_refs: The Nederlandse Montessori Vereniging, founded 1917

stops.name: Rome, the meeting with Mussolini
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1924; the meeting venue is not identified in the sources and the pin stands near the seat of government. The honorary presidency dates from 1926
stops.campa: She meets Benito Mussolini, two years into his government, and comes away with the state behind her: official sponsorship of Montessori teacher training, public money, the friends' society reorganised as the Opera Nazionale Montessori under royal charter, and from 1926 the Duce himself as its honorary president. He wants literacy and a modern schoolroom that reflects well on the regime. She wants her method taught correctly and at national scale. Each of them takes the other for the instrument.
stops.quote: All human victories, all human progress, stand upon the inner force.
stops.quote_source: Maria Montessori, The Montessori Method (1912), on prizes and punishments
suggested_refs: The Opera Nazionale Montessori, chartered under the Fascist state; mussolini.journey.json

stops.name: Elsinore, the founding of the Association Montessori Internationale
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1929; month and day not recorded. The AMI timeline records that the association's headquarters were in Berlin until 1935 and in Amsterdam thereafter, a Berlin period the research pool omitted
stops.campa: At the first International Montessori Congress, at Elsinore in Denmark, she and Mario found the Association Montessori Internationale to hold the standards: who may train teachers, who may manufacture the material, who may use the name. Its first offices are in Berlin. The movement has outrun any one person's supervision and she has decided that it will be supervised regardless. The story that she gave her method freely away to humanity has to be read against the constitution of this body.
suggested_refs: The founding statutes of the Association Montessori Internationale, Elsinore 1929
sources: AMI Montessori Archives, 'Timeline: Maria Montessori's Life'

stops.name: Geneva, education as the making of peace
stops.date_confidence: 1932 attested for Geneva and Nice; the further peace congresses at Brussels, Copenhagen and Utrecht are dated by en.wikipedia only to the span 1932 to 1939, and the research pool's separate 1937 Copenhagen date is unsupported
stops.campa: At the International Peace Club she argues that peace is not the interval between wars and cannot be manufactured by treaties, that it has to be built inside the person, and that the only workshop for the job is the education of small children. She is sixty-two. The League of Nations sits a mile up the lake and Europe is preparing the other thing. She speaks in the same years at Nice, at Brussels, at Copenhagen and at Utrecht, and those lectures are collected afterwards as Educazione e pace.
suggested_refs: Maria Montessori, Educazione e pace, collecting the peace lectures of 1932 to 1939

stops.name: Rome, the surveillance and the break
stops.date_confidence: attested; the surveillance is dated 1932 and the resignation from the Opera Nazionale Montessori 1933, the two compressed into one stop
stops.campa: By 1932 she and Mario are under political surveillance by the Fascist authorities. The bargain has failed over the thing it was always going to fail over: who controls the training of the teachers, and whether children in a Montessori classroom will wear the uniform of the Balilla and swear the oath. She resigns from the Opera Nazionale Montessori. Over the next two years the regime absorbs or closes what remains of the Montessori schools in Italy, and the books are taken out of the shops.
suggested_refs: Italian police surveillance files on Maria and Mario Montessori, 1932

stops.name: Barcelona, out of Italy
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1934; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: She leaves Italy for Barcelona as the Italian institutions carrying her name are shut or swallowed. She is sixty-four. Everything she built in her own country between 1907 and 1934 now belongs to a state she has quarrelled with, and the work goes on in Catalonia, in the Netherlands, in England, in India, anywhere that is not Rome. Mario travels with her, as he will from here on, with the trunks of apparatus and the correspondence. She does not live in Italy again.
suggested_refs: The dissolution of the Italian Montessori institutions, 1933 to 1936

stops.name: Port of Barcelona, the flight from the coup
stops.date_confidence: the departure is attested to 1936, following the coup of 18 July; no source consulted dates it to a day, and 19 July is used here only to order the segment. The British warship is movement tradition, absent from both en.wikipedia and the AMI timeline
stops.campa: Franco's generals rise in July and Barcelona goes to the barricades. The family leaves in haste, twenty years of a life in the city ended inside a week. She is sixty-five, displaced for the second time in two years. The movement's own telling has a British warship taking her off; no contemporaneous source consulted here carries it, and the AMI timeline says only that she fled Barcelona for England. What the sources agree on is that she got out. By what means, and with whose help, is not on record.
suggested_refs: The evacuation of foreign nationals from Barcelona, July 1936
sources: AMI Montessori Archives, 'Timeline: Maria Montessori's Life'

stops.name: London, the crossing out of Spain
stops.date_confidence: the England leg is attested by en.wikipedia, which states that the family left Barcelona for England before moving to Laren; no source consulted gives a date, an address or a length of stay, and August 1936 is used only to order the segment
stops.campa: They land in England, and in England the trail thins to nothing. The London training courses and the English societies are reason enough to stop there, but no source consulted names a street, a month or a length of stay, and the compressed accounts drop the leg altogether and carry her straight from Spain to Holland. It is a gap in the record of a very well documented life, and it falls in the year she needed shelter most. She is sixty-five, she has left a school and a laboratory behind in a city at war, and she is being put up by people whose names nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: The Montessori societies and training courses in England, 1930s
sources: AMI Montessori Archives, 'Timeline: Maria Montessori's Life'

stops.name: Laren, the house on the heath
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1936 for the settlement at Laren, near Amsterdam; month and day not recorded, and October is used here only to place it after the England leg
stops.campa: The family settles at Laren, a village of heath and painters east of Amsterdam, in the country that founded a Montessori society nineteen years ago and has schools enough to keep her busy. It is meant as a base. It turns out to be a way station: within three years she is on a ship to Madras. She is sixty-six and has moved her household four times in three years, each time one step ahead of a government. The manuscripts and the material travel with her.
suggested_refs: The Montessori household at Laren, North Holland, 1936 to 1939

stops.name: Adyar, the Theosophical compound
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1939; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. Her 1899 membership of the Theosophical Society's European Section comes from the background dossier and is not independently confirmed
stops.campa: The Theosophical Society invites her to Adyar, outside Madras, to give a training course, and she and Mario take ship for India. The compound is a river-mouth estate of banyan and libraries, headquarters of an international society whose European section she had joined forty years before. She is sixty-eight and comes for a season's teaching. Hundreds of Indian students enrol. Europe goes to war while the course is running, and she stays seven years.
suggested_refs: The Theosophical Society headquarters at Adyar, Madras

stops.name: Adyar, the enemy alien
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1940 for Italy's entry into the war and the internment; day not recorded
stops.campa: Italy declares war in June and the British authorities in India classify the Montessoris as enemy aliens. Mario is interned. His mother, a few weeks short of seventy, is confined to the Theosophical compound and told she may not leave it. Petitions are made on her birthday and Mario is returned to her after roughly two months. The popular version has her spending seven years in an Indian prison. She spends them in a walled garden she cannot leave, teaching.
suggested_refs: British Indian enemy-alien internment records, 1940

stops.name: Kodaikanal, cosmic education
stops.date_confidence: 1942 attested for the cosmic-education work; the Kodaikanal internment is dated 1942 to 1944 by it.wikipedia, while en.wikipedia says only that she remained in Madras and Kodaikanal until 1946, so the research pool's 1940 to 1946 range for Kodaikanal alone is too wide
stops.campa: In the Palani hills, seven thousand feet above the plain, the restricted years turn productive. She works out the four planes of development, the whole arc from birth to twenty-four, and the scheme she calls cosmic education: give the six-year-old not a subject but the universe, the making of the earth, the coming of life, the coming of the human being, and let the particulars find their places inside it afterwards. Mario builds and orders the lessons. She talks, and he writes and makes.
stops.quote: The child in reality is not resting, he is performing the mysterious inner work of his autoformation.
stops.quote_source: Maria Montessori, Dr. Montessori's Own Handbook (1914), introductory remarks
suggested_refs: The Kodaikanal courses and the origins of the cosmic-education curriculum

stops.name: Ceylon, the thirty lectures
stops.date_confidence: 1944 attested for the journey and for the granting of freedom of movement; en.wikipedia names only Sri Lanka and no city, so the Colombo pin is a reconstruction and the month is unrecorded
stops.campa: In 1944 the restrictions loosen far enough for travel and she crosses to Ceylon, giving some thirty lectures on the first years of life and a training course the government there recognises. She is seventy-three. The Indian and Ceylonese years make her something the European years never did, a teacher of teachers working through interpreters on a continent not her own. The following year she is at Jaipur for the first All India Montessori Conference.
suggested_refs: The 1944 Ceylon lecture series and government-recognised training course

stops.name: London, the return to Europe
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1946; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: After the war she returns to Europe and gives a training course in London, and a Montessori Centre opens in the city the year after. Europe has to be rebuilt, schools included, and there is nobody else living who can say with authority what the method is and is not. She is seventy-six. Italy, having taken the Opera Nazionale Montessori from her in 1933, now asks her help in putting it back together, and she agrees to that as well. The teachers who come to the London course she takes through the same sequence she used on Via dei Marsi, in the same order.
suggested_refs: The London Montessori Centre, opened 1947

stops.name: Ahmedabad, the book she did not write
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1947 for the Adyar and Ahmedabad courses; month and day not recorded. The Absorbent Mind's composition from student transcripts is standard in the literature
stops.campa: She returns to India, to Adyar and then to Ahmedabad in Gujarat, and lectures to students who take down what she says. Those notes are edited afterwards into The Absorbent Mind, the book by which most of the English-speaking world knows her and which she never sat down to write: it is the transcript of a woman in her late seventies talking, in a language learned late, to a room full of teachers on the other side of the world from San Lorenzo. The absorbent mind of the title is the youngest child's, the one that takes in a language and a world without being taught either.
stops.quote: The control of the error lies in the material itself, and the child has concrete evidence of it.
stops.quote_source: Maria Montessori, Dr. Montessori's Own Handbook (1914), 'Sensory Education'
suggested_refs: The Absorbent Mind, edited from the Adyar and Ahmedabad course transcripts

stops.name: Karachi, the last of the Indian years
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1949; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Two years after partition she gives a training course at Karachi and a Pakistan Montessori Association is founded around it. The subcontinent she came to for one season has given her two national movements and the last decade of her working life. She is seventy-eight and travels as she has travelled since 1934, with a son, a trunk of apparatus and a schedule of courses booked further ahead than her body will carry her. Nine years earlier the British authorities would not let her out of a walled garden at Adyar. This is the last course she gives on the subcontinent.
suggested_refs: The Pakistan Montessori Association, founded 1949

segments.name: The Last Courses and the Grave at Noordwijk

stops.name: Sanremo, the congress and the nominations
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1949 for the eighth congress; month not recorded. The research pool's count of the Nobel nominations is wrong: en.wikipedia and the AMI timeline agree on nominations in 1949, 1950 and 1951, six in total
stops.campa: The eighth International Montessori Congress meets at Sanremo on the Ligurian coast, and the country that shut her method down fifteen years earlier receives her as a national figure. Delegates arrive from the countries where the method survived the war and from several where it did not. She is seventy-eight, and has come home to a republic, to a coast an hour from the French border she crossed the other way in 1934. The same year brings the first of her nominations for the Nobel Peace Prize, with further nominations in 1950 and in 1951, six in all across the three years. She does not win any of them.
suggested_refs: The eighth International Montessori Congress, Sanremo 1949; Nobel Peace Prize nomination archive
sources: AMI Montessori Archives, 'Timeline: Maria Montessori's Life'

stops.name: Amsterdam, the year of the honours
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1949 for the Legion of Honour, the Order of Orange-Nassau and the Amsterdam honorary doctorate; no month is recorded for any of the three, and June is used only to order the segment
stops.campa: France makes her a member of the Legion of Honour. The Netherlands appoints her Officer of the Order of Orange-Nassau. The University of Amsterdam gives her an honorary doctorate, the medical faculty of Rome having taken six years to let her in. She is seventy-nine and collecting inside one calendar year the recognitions that borrowed countries can offer a foreigner. Her own country's honours came earlier, from a government she then had to break with.
suggested_refs: The 1949 honours: Legion d'honneur, Order of Orange-Nassau, University of Amsterdam honorary doctorate

stops.name: Florence, UNESCO and the plainest claim
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1950 for the UNESCO-associated conference at Florence and the twenty-ninth international training course at Perugia; months not recorded
stops.campa: She represents Italy at a UNESCO conference in Florence, the city her father's postings brought her to at the age of three, and makes the argument she has been making since Geneva in 1932: that peace is a work of construction and that its material is the child. The same year she gives the twenty-ninth international training course at Perugia. She is eighty, and still standing in front of rooms of teachers, going through the apparatus piece by piece, in the order the children use it.
suggested_refs: The 1950 UNESCO conference at Florence; the twenty-ninth international training course, Perugia

stops.name: Wiesbaden, the governing board
stops.date_confidence: attested to 19 June 1951
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of June she attends a preliminary meeting of the UNESCO governing board at Wiesbaden. It is a committee room, an agenda, a list of names to be circulated afterwards. There is nothing to say about the day except that she crossed Germany at eighty to sit in it, and that the minutes record her presence among the delegates. The international bodies are being assembled again, six years after the war, out of the people who survived it. Fifty-five years ago she stood in Berlin at twenty-six, arguing the wages of women before a congress, in a German state that no longer exists in any form.
suggested_refs: Minutes of the preliminary meeting of the UNESCO Governing Board, Wiesbaden, 19 June 1951

stops.name: London, the ninth congress and the last courses
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1951 for the ninth International Montessori Congress in London and for the Innsbruck training course; no months are recorded and September is used only to order the segment
stops.campa: She takes part in the ninth International Montessori Congress in London and gives a training course at Innsbruck the same year. These are the last of both. Fifty-two years earlier she came to London as a young doctor to speak about women's wages and the sulphur children of Sicily and was presented to Queen Victoria; she comes back at eighty-one to certify teachers, and Mario handles the arrangements. Between the two visits sit a medical practice, two world wars, a Fascist patronage and its collapse, and an internment in India. She goes home to Holland afterwards.
suggested_refs: The ninth International Montessori Congress, London 1951; the Innsbruck training course of 1951

stops.name: Noordwijk aan Zee, the afternoon of the sixth of May
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: She is staying with Mario in a house at Noordwijk aan Zee on the Dutch coast, and there is an invitation on the table to travel to Africa and open the work there. She is eighty-one and considering it. She had said for years that she wished to be buried wherever death happened to find her rather than carried back to Italy, and it finds her here, in the country she first lectured in thirty-five years ago. On the sixth of May a cerebral hemorrhage kills her, quickly, in the house.
suggested_refs: The Montessori house at Noordwijk aan Zee
sources: AMI Montessori Archives, 'Inscription on Maria Montessori's Grave'

stops.name: Noordwijk, the grave with the inscription addressed to children
stops.date_confidence: the burial at the Roman Catholic cemetery of Noordwijk is attested; no source consulted gives the date of the funeral, and 10 May is used only to place it after the death. The inscription's wording differs between sources: the AMI archive renders the engraved text with construzione, it.wikipedia with the standard costruzione and added commas
stops.campa: They bury her in the Roman Catholic cemetery at Noordwijk, in a semicircular monument designed by her eldest grandson, Mario Montessori Jr., and cut into it an Italian sentence addressed not to mourners but to children. The Italian on the stone is not quite the Italian of the dictionaries, and the two spellings are both in print. Her house on the Koninginneweg in Amsterdam becomes the archive; the Association Montessori Internationale is still there.
stops.quote: Io prego i cari bambini che possono tutto di unirsi a me per la construzione della pace negli uomini e nel mondo.
stops.quote_source: Inscription on Maria Montessori's grave, Noordwijk, as rendered by the AMI Montessori Archives
suggested_refs: The Montessori grave in the Roman Catholic cemetery at Noordwijk; the AMI archive at Koninginneweg 161, Amsterdam
sources: AMI Montessori Archives, 'Inscription on Maria Montessori's Grave'
